narrative.overview:
The report should feel like an accessibility triage room already in motion: decisive enough for a release conversation, calm enough for sustained evidence review, and rigorous enough that every conclusion can be traced. An editorial hierarchy turns a dense technical record into a readable sequence of status, tested strengths, priority, proposed change, effort, and proof.

This is an evidence surface, not a scanner dashboard. Warm paper, deep forest decision fields, ruled rows, compact notation, and large display language establish authority without substituting decoration for evidence. Density increases deliberately as the reviewer moves from the first decision viewport into the technical annex.
keyCharacteristics: Decisive, scoped status language rather than a universal score.
Editorial display type paired with restrained, highly legible interface text.
Evidence imagery and proposed states presented as review material, never decoration.
Ruled rows and tonal layering instead of ornamental panels or dashboard chrome.
Responsive reading order that preserves every claim and its proof.

rules.name: The Meaning Before Mood Rule
rules.body: Semantic colors communicate a tested result or interaction state; never use them merely to make a section more colorful.

rules.name: The No Score Gradient Rule
rules.body: Never turn the report into a red-to-green accessibility percentage or imply coverage beyond the authored scenario.

rules.name: The Decision Has a Voice Rule
rules.body: Display type states the assessment and its hierarchy; body type explains it. Do not set whole interfaces or long technical passages in the display face.

rules.name: The Portable Face Rule
rules.body: Ship the display font with the report and retain the defined fallback stack so the hierarchy does not depend on a reviewer’s installed fonts.

rules.name: The Decision-to-Detail Rule
rules.body: Begin spacious and decisive, then allow density to rise as the reader enters evidence and the annex.

rules.name: The Reading Order Rule
rules.body: Responsive layouts may stack, scroll, or regroup, but they never hide evidence or rearrange the semantic reading order.

rules.name: The Ruled Surface Rule
rules.body: Use a line, tone, or dark field to establish hierarchy. A shadow is not part of this report language.

rules.name: The Radius Has Meaning Rule
rules.body: Large corners belong to decision zones, medium corners to bounded evidence, compact corners to controls, and pills to terse semantic labels or filters.

dos: Do lead with the scoped release decision, confirmed issue count, positive tested behaviors, and focused effort.
Do use ruled rows and tonal surfaces to organize dense evidence.
Do magnify or annotate affected regions and keep a route to the full capture.
Do preserve visible keyboard focus, semantic labels, and the same evidence in every responsive layout.
Do keep conversational answers local to captured evidence and visibly bounded by the authored scenario.
donts: Don't present an accessibility percentage, universal conformance claim, or certainty the evidence does not support.
Don't use decorative gradients, ornamental shadows, or generic dashboard card grids.
Don't present a simulated proposal as an implemented result.
Don't hide technical proof to simplify mobile layouts; linearize it or make wide tables scroll.
Don't use semantic status colors as ambient decoration.
